content:
The biggest highlight of the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 is all on the inside. Most importantly, there's a brand-new health sensing system, bringing the biggest health tracking improvement in Apple Watch in years.

I've been using the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 for the past week. Here's everything you need to know.

  • Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $390 (original price $399)
  • Apple Watch Ultra 4 in black starts at $780 (original price $799)

Design

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 look identical to the previous generation at first glance. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 still comes in two titanium case options: natural and black. My review unit is the natural color.

As for the Apple Watch Series 12, the real design story is in the colors and cases.

First, the dimensions of the Apple Watch Series 12 have changed slightly. Apple's tech specs page shows the display area is about 2% smaller than the Series 10 and Series 11. However, the total pixel count hasn't changed. With the display area slightly reduced, the Apple Watch Series 12 case is about 1mm wider.

In actual use, you can't feel these differences at all. The Apple Watch display still extends close to the edge of the case. Considering the redesigned health sensing system (more on that below), it's truly impressive that Apple was able to maintain this design.

The Apple Watch Series 12 comes in three materials: aluminum, titanium, and ceramic.

Aluminum comes in four case colors: deep bronze, light gold, black, and space gray. The aluminum version's display glass has also been changed from Ion-X to Ceramic Shield 2.

My Apple Watch Series 12 review unit is the black aluminum version. Unlike last year's jet black aluminum case, the Apple Watch Series 12 black has a matte texture. I personally prefer the look of the jet black, but I understand Apple switches up the style every year, and jet black may come back in the future.

Last week I got to try all the colors of the Apple Watch Series 12 aluminum in person, and the most eye-catching was the deep bronze. This color is very elegant and unlike any aluminum Apple Watch before it. Light gold is also a great choice for those who like gold. There's no silver aluminum Apple Watch Series 12, but the space gray is light enough that I think it should be acceptable for most people.

The Apple Watch Series 12 titanium version comes in two case colors: brilliant gold and natural. By comparison, the titanium Apple Watch Series 11 came in natural, gold, and slate gray.

The brilliant gold is very striking. From the appearance and how it differs from last year's colors, I think Apple's goal is clear: they want to make the titanium Apple Watch Series 12 look like real gold, without actually using real gold. Although opinions on what "real gold" should look like vary, in my eyes, Apple did a great job with the Series 12's brilliant gold titanium.

Last but not least, the Apple Watch Series 12 ceramic version comes in two case colors: midnight blue and pearl white. The last time Apple released a ceramic watch was the 2019 Series 5, and it quickly became a fan favorite.

At last week's Apple event, I only had a few minutes to try the ceramic Apple Watch Series 12. The midnight blue is quite nice, but the moment I saw the pearl white, I was immediately drawn to it. It's not as white as the Series 5; depending on the lighting, it has a slightly soft off-white sheen.

Health Tracking

The biggest change in the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the brand-new health sensing system, which I believe is the biggest upgrade to Apple Watch's health features in years.

This starts with a completely new design of the sensing hardware. Apple mentions three aspects:

  • The electrode contact area is larger, but the sensor itself hasn't gotten bigger, resulting in better skin contact during ECG readings.
  • The photodiodes have been redesigned, now arranged in a ring shape to capture more reflected light.
  • The green LED is larger, making readings more reliable when you're moving, and also more power-efficient.

This allows the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 to perform more accurate and frequent background heart rate measurements. This means more heart rate readings even when you're not exercising.

Previous Apple Watch models mainly tried to measure background heart rate about every five minutes while you were at rest.

Apple says the new health sensing system provides "the most accurate heart rate sensing in any wearable device." In a study with over 1,000 participants, Apple says the Series 12's overall accuracy during exercise and daily activities is statistically better than all competing wearable devices they tested.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 have major improvements. They measure your heart rate every five seconds, whether you're moving or at rest. Such frequent and accurate heart rate readings can bring more data and insights.

Previous Apple Watch models only measured heart rate every five minutes while at rest, which itself was a blind spot. They might miss the moment your heart rate rises when you're not exercising, or only randomly pick up one or two readings during that time.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 don't just take more readings—they can read even when you're moving. You can clearly see the impact on heart rate from activities like carrying groceries, doing yard work, or shoveling snow.

Apple has also added several new ways to view your heart rate data. First, the heart rate app on Apple Watch has been redesigned so you can see your heart rate and a chart of readings from the past two minutes.

Two new heart rate complications have also been added to the watch face, letting you see your heart rate at a glance.

Having used the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 for a week, I've found this extra data very enlightening. I have a much better understanding of how the little things I do during the day affect my heart rate. For example, I can imagine the impact of an afternoon tea or a stressful moment at work.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 don't just give you more raw data—they also actively leverage more frequent heart rate readings to support new features and improvements.

First, Apple says this data makes calorie estimation more accurate. I haven't seen any major changes in my own data yet, but it may become clearer after wearing it for more than a week.

I was hoping that more frequent heart rate measurements would improve automatic workout detection. At least in my testing so far, I haven't seen this happen.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 now also sample heart rate variability (HRV) at a higher frequency. Previously HRV was only read every two hours, but the new Apple Watch models can read it as frequently as every five minutes when at rest.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 now also track Recovery HRV, which is best suited for identifying daily stress and fatigue signals. The new Apple Watch models also continue to measure overall HRV as before, which is best suited for identifying broader health signals.

Additionally, Apple has integrated Recovery HRV measurement into the overnight "Vitals" report.

Vitals

Speaking of Vitals, Apple has made several changes to the entire Vitals experience on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. First, Vitals has added a daytime view.

Previously Vitals was only an overnight report that you'd see the next morning. The daytime view shows your daytime heart rate and HRV, with the concept being that you can see if something's off without waiting for the overnight report.

Vitals will also categorize your metrics into four categories: significantly low, slightly low, typical, or good. Compared to the previous two-tier system—which only categorized metrics as typical or out of range—this provides more granular classification.

I really love the Vitals app on Apple Watch, and I'm glad to see Apple making meaningful improvements on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. It often detects signs of illness before I actually get sick.

The new daytime view needs more testing to know how practical it is, since it only covers two metrics. However, Vitals has several good improvements that make good use of the more frequent heart rate and HRV measurements brought by the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Readiness

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 offer a new readiness score, aimed at condensing all the data Apple Watch has on you into a single score.

Apple says readiness takes into account your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score. The readiness score also updates throughout the day based on new data from naps, activity, and daytime heart rate, so it dynamically adjusts as new data comes in.

You can see the readiness score in the Readiness app on Apple Watch, as well as in the Fitness app on iPhone. It's also available in the newly redesigned Health app, which is currently in beta testing.

Apple Watch's biggest competitors have offered similar scores for a few years now, including Whoop (Whoop Recovery) and Oura (Readiness Score). The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are the first to include a readiness feature, making it the most direct response to other wearables from Apple to date.

I've been wearing an Oura Ring for the past year, mainly for its readiness score. I love having a number that condenses different metrics into one figure that you can glance at each morning. This has always been a major gap in the Apple Watch software experience, and I'm glad Apple is now taking a similar approach.

Apple Watch's readiness score requires a week of sleep data, but my review unit has only had one week. That means I've only gotten one readiness score so far, so I can't yet conclude how practical Apple's version is.

Looking at the data Apple uses to calculate readiness, I'm somewhat optimistic. I also think Apple made the right call using a 0-10 scoring scale, rather than Oura's 0-100 score. Apple's readiness ranges are as follows:

  • 0-1: Recover
  • 2-4: Pace Yourself
  • 5-7: Ready
  • 8-10: Go For It

I find these fairly straightforward, and probably more practical than the scores and somewhat preachy (or passive-aggressive) advice Oura provides. Looking forward to continuing testing over the next few weeks and directly comparing scores with Oura.

For comparison, on a day when my Apple Watch readiness score was 8/10, my Oura Ring was 85/100.

I also like that readiness shows which factors pushed your score up or down, whether it's sleep, activity, or overnight vitals, and you can tap into the relevant apps to see details.

Performance

Both the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12 use Apple's brand-new S11 chip, which Apple describes as "the most powerful wearable chip yet."

This is the first truly new chip in Apple Watch since the S9 chip debuted in the Apple Watch Series 9 in 2023. The S10 chip in the Apple Watch Series 10 was just a thinner package version of the same design, and last year's models had no new chip at all.

Apple emphasizes that the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine components in the new S11 chip are derived from the A20 Pro chip used in the iPhone 18 Pro. Apple Watch's RAM is also reportedly doubled from 2GB to 4GB.

The S11 chip also has another component: a new always-on processor that can handle complex tasks without needing to engage the main chip. Inside it has a secure enclive—a hardware-isolated space specifically for securely storing Audio Intelligence's microphone data.

Apple says the S11 chip combined with the always-on processor actually plays a role in several features on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4:

  • It works together with the brand-new health sensing system to provide higher frequency heart rate readings.
  • It helps support Audio Intelligence features like Siri Recap (more on that below).
  • It runs a redesigned step counter model, which Apple says is more accurate even when your arm isn't moving (e.g., pushing a stroller).

Compared with my Apple Watch Ultra 3, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12 are noticeably faster at opening new apps, scrolling menus, and basic Siri AI interactions. But for me, what's most impressive is the important role it plays in supporting the new health features mentioned above.

Battery Life

The Apple Watch Series 12 comes with a slightly larger battery, paired with the greater efficiency of the health sensing system and S11 chip. Here are Apple's battery life claims for the Apple Watch Series 12:

  • 24 hours of normal use (same as Series 11)
  • 38 hours in Low Power Mode (same as Series 11)
  • 10 hours of outdoor workout, 2 hours more than the previous generation

Apple also highlights faster charging in certain scenarios:

  • 5 minutes of fast charging provides up to 10 hours of sleep tracking
  • 15 minutes of fast charging provides up to 12 hours of battery life
  • About 30 minutes to charge to 80% (same as previous generation)

While testing the Apple Watch Series 12, the first two items above stood out particularly. Apple Watch is increasingly focused on sleep tracking, and being able to quickly charge before bed is very important.

As for the Apple Watch Ultra 4, which also features a larger battery, Apple says:

  • 50 hours of normal use, up from Ultra 3's 42 hours
  • 84 hours in Low Power Mode, up from Ultra 3's 72 hours
  • Workout: 18 hours standard (14 hours on previous gen), 25 hours extended (20 hours on previous gen), up to 45 hours maximum extended
  • 15 minutes of fast charging provides up to 18 hours of battery life, up from Ultra 3's 12 hours

I tested the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and it really does meet Apple's battery life claims. In real-world testing, I charged it to 100% around 8 PM on Sunday night, and didn't need to charge again until 8 PM on Tuesday night. That's 48 hours on a single charge, including 90 minutes of workout tracking, 3 hours away from iPhone, and 2 nights of sleep tracking.

Other Details

  • A new "Steps" complication has been added to the watch face, with real-time step count updates. I love it.
  • Apple has redesigned the Apple Watch Ultra's Ocean Band. It now uses semi-transparent silicone material, available in semi-transparent gray, semi-transparent sea kelp green, and semi-transparent black. Beyond the different look, the new Ocean Band also feels lighter on the wrist.
  • A new Siri Modular watch face has been added, also compatible with older models. Zac has a detailed introduction here.

Coming Soon

This is actually just the beginning of this year's Apple Watch.

First, Apple is in the process of redesigning a brand-new version of the Health app, adding a "Longevity" tab and indicators like "Health Age." I'm really looking forward to trying the new Health app. Apple says the new Health app will be available in a software update later this year, with a beta version available starting Wednesday afternoon.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will also add new Audio Intelligence features later this year, including Live Rewind and Siri Recap.

Live Rewind lets you quickly double-press the Digital Crown to review the past 15 seconds of conversation as text snippets. Siri Recap, on the other hand, generates high-level summaries of conversations for you to review later. Apple says both features will be available in beta later this year. The company has also established comprehensive privacy policies for these features.

Along with the rollout of Siri AI, Siri Recap and Live Rewind represent Apple's biggest step in turning Apple Watch into a true AI wearable—and I'm very much looking forward to seeing how this develops.

9to5Mac's Take

Who should upgrade to the Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4? I think this is one of the most substantial upgrades in recent years. If you're currently using a Series 9 or Ultra 2 (or older), I would seriously consider upgrading. If you already have a newer Apple Watch, it depends on how much you care about the new health features.

On the surface, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 may seem like only minor updates. They don't completely change the form factor (although the new color and material options are quite nice).

Instead, it's the inside that makes the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 so interesting. Apple has focused on making the watch stronger in the areas it's already best at: being an all-day companion that can monitor your heart, sleep, and activity. Oh, and keeping you connected with friends, family, and the outside world.

The new health sensing system is the foundation of everything. It fundamentally changes how much your Apple Watch knows about you throughout the day.

Importantly, Apple hasn't just increased the frequency of heart rate readings and left it to you to digest all that extra data. The new hardware works together with watchOS 27 to provide meaningful insights into your daily life, including a promising Readiness app and a more powerful Vitals app.

Throw in the Siri Recap and Live Rewind features coming later this year, and the story gets even more exciting. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 not only know more about you than ever before, but also help you stay on top of the world around you.

Overall, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 provide the clearest signal yet of where Apple's most important wearable is headed.
